title: India Just Opened Its Stock Market to Every Foreigner on Earth. Here Is What Changed Overnight.
excerpt: A sweeping FEMA amendment notified on June 12 replaces the NRI-only investment framework with one that lets any individual residing outside India buy and sell listed Indian equities — a historic shift in capital account liberalisation.
body:
For as long as India has had a stock market worth investing in, the rules about who gets to participate from abroad have been drawn along lines of heritage. Non-Resident Indians. Overseas Citizens of India. People of Indian Origin. If you had an Indian passport, an OCI card, or at least a PIO status, you could buy shares on the BSE and NSE through designated bank branches. Everyone else was locked out unless they registered as a Foreign Portfolio Investor with SEBI — a process involving compliance costs, custodial arrangements, and regulatory overhead that made it practical only for institutional players.

On June 12, the Indian government quietly changed that. Forever.

The Ministry of Finance notified the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) (Third Amendment) Rules, 2026, replacing the entire framework governing overseas individual investment in Indian equities. The amendment does not merely tweak limits or simplify forms. It rewrites the eligibility criteria from the ground up.

What Actually Changed

The amendment replaces "a Non-Resident Indian or an Overseas Citizen of India" throughout the FEMA rules with a broader term: "an individual person resident outside India." Chapter V of the principal rules has been renamed from "Investment by Non-Resident Indian or an Overseas Citizen of India" to "Investment by an Individual Person Resident Outside India Including a Non-Resident Indian or an Overseas Citizen of India."

The practical effect: a British software engineer in London, a Japanese entrepreneur in Tokyo, or a Brazilian fund manager in São Paulo can now buy shares of Reliance, HDFC Bank, or Infosys through a designated branch of an authorised dealer bank in India — the same route previously reserved for NRIs.

Amended Rule 12 now permits any individual residing outside India to purchase or sell equity instruments of listed Indian companies on a repatriation basis, subject to Schedule III conditions.

The Limits and Safeguards

This is not a free-for-all. The government has retained critical guardrails.

"Foreign investors have pulled over $30 billion from Indian equities in 2026, accelerated by the US-Iran conflict's impact on crude prices and hot US inflation."

The individual investment cap remains at less than 10 per cent of a listed company's paid-up equity capital on a fully diluted basis. The aggregate holding of all non-resident individuals under this route cannot exceed 24 per cent unless sectoral regulations permit otherwise.

If an individual breaches the 10 per cent threshold, they have five trading days to divest the excess. If they choose not to divest, the entire holding is reclassified as Foreign Direct Investment — triggering FDI norms, sectoral caps, and potentially requiring government approval.

Investments from countries sharing a land border with India — primarily China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, and Myanmar — still require prior government approval when they result in transfer of ownership or control.

Why Now

The timing is strategic. India is fighting two battles simultaneously: a weak rupee and record foreign portfolio outflows. Foreign investors have pulled over $30 billion from Indian equities in 2026, accelerated by the US-Iran conflict's impact on crude prices and hot US inflation.

Just a week earlier, the RBI doubled NRI individual investment limits from 5 to 10 per cent and raised the aggregate ceiling from 10 to 24 per cent. The FEMA amendment extends those expanded limits to everyone.

"It is a step in the right direction, but needs to be complemented by simple and digital processes related to KYC, taxation, repatriation for significant inflows to materialise," said Nilesh Shah, managing director at Kotak Mahindra Asset Management.

The caution is warranted. NRI holdings currently represent just 0.7 per cent of Sensex market capitalisation — roughly Rs 5.2 lakh crore against a total market cap of Rs 461 lakh crore. Even doubling or tripling that through broader participation would not solve India's capital flow problem overnight.

What NRIs Should Know

For existing NRI investors, the immediate impact is indirect but significant.

First, the playing field just got wider. Companies that NRIs hold may now see additional buying interest from non-Indian foreign individuals, potentially supporting valuations. But they may also see the 24 per cent aggregate ceiling fill faster, which could constrain future NRI purchases in popular stocks.

Second, the RBI's parallel FCNR deposit scheme — offering banks zero hedging cost on dollar deposits — is creating a separate pull for NRI capital. According to Emkay Global Financial Services, leveraged FCNR strategies could yield returns exceeding 20 per cent on invested capital. The combination of equity access and fixed-income incentives makes this an unusually active window for NRI financial decisions.

Third, documentation and KYC remain friction points. The policy direction is clear, but market participants warn that implementation — particularly around tax treaty benefits, capital gains withholding, and repatriation timelines — will determine whether foreign individuals actually show up.

The Bigger Picture

India's capital markets have been gradually liberalising for three decades, but always with a preference for institutional over individual foreign participation. This amendment breaks that pattern. It says, in effect, that an individual with a bank account and a broker need not prove Indian heritage to own a piece of India's growth story.

Gopal Jain, Managing Director and CEO of Gaja Alternative Asset Management, called the move one that connects India's capital markets more closely with global savings and "should be viewed as a measured step towards further capital account liberalisation."

For NRIs, the emotional valence is complex. The exclusive access that once came with diaspora identity is now shared with the world. But if it brings more capital, more liquidity, and more stability to the markets their own savings depend on, the trade-off may be worth it.

The notification number is 1/11/2025-EM, dated June 12, 2026. The rules are effective immediately.
nri_angle: NRIs already invested in Indian equities now share the playing field with every foreign individual globally — understanding the new rules, limits, and safeguards is essential to protect existing holdings.
author: Diaspora Desk
